image.alt: A black ZZ plant in a white pot, its arching stems lined with paired glossy leaflets in near-black green

light.label: Bright indirect light
light.note: Survives low light, but the leaves stay green instead of blackening

landscape_use.note: Frost-free zones, out of direct sun

snap: The dark form of the ZZ plant, its paired glossy leaflets opening bright lime green and hardening to a near-black purple. It stores water in underground rhizomes and shrugs off neglect that would kill most houseplants, and every part of it is toxic if chewed.

deep_dive.title: Origin & Habit
deep_dive.body: A dark-leaved selection of Zamioculcas zamiifolia, the East African species behind the ordinary green ZZ. It was raised in South Korea and reached the trade as 'Raven' in 2018. The habit is unchanged: fat water-storing rhizomes below the soil, arching stems to about two feet, and growth that arrives in occasional flushes rather than steadily.

deep_dive.title: Key Care Rule
deep_dive.body: Let the mix dry out completely, then water it thoroughly. The rhizomes are a reservoir, and a mix kept damp rots them — this is very nearly the only way to kill a ZZ. In a dim corner it may want water just once a month, so judge by the soil rather than the calendar.

deep_dive.title: Special Feature
deep_dive.body: New growth opens bright lime green and darkens over several weeks to near-black, so a plant in growth carries both colours at once. A pale green stem is not a reversion or a mislabelled plant — it is simply new, and the colour arrives on its own. Brighter indirect light makes it go darker; a dim corner keeps it green.
